articles.title: Large language models
articles.definition: An LLM learns a distribution over token sequences, enabling conditional text generation rather than database lookup.
articles.explanation: An LLM learns a distribution over token sequences, enabling conditional text generation rather than database lookup. Training adjusts parameters to predict text; inference conditions each next-token distribution on the prompt and prior output. Fluent continuation is useful for language tasks but does not establish factual truth.

articles.title: Tokens and tokenization
articles.definition: Tokens are vocabulary units such as subwords, punctuation, or bytes; they are not necessarily words.
articles.explanation: Tokens are vocabulary units such as subwords, punctuation, or bytes; they are not necessarily words. A tokenizer maps text to IDs and the model predicts IDs that are decoded back to text. Language and code can have different token densities, affecting both context limits and latency.

articles.title: Transformer attention
articles.definition: Attention forms contextual representations by weighting value vectors according to query-key compatibility.
articles.explanation: Attention forms contextual representations by weighting value vectors according to query-key compatibility. Scaled dot-product attention computes softmax(QK transpose / sqrt(d))V; causal masks prevent attending to future tokens during autoregressive training. Dense attention mixes information effectively but its pairwise interactions grow quadratically with sequence length.

articles.title: Embeddings and cosine similarity
articles.definition: An embedding is a learned vector representation; cosine similarity measures angle rather than vector magnitude.
articles.explanation: An embedding is a learned vector representation; cosine similarity measures angle rather than vector magnitude. For vectors u and v, cosine equals dot(u,v)/(norm(u)norm(v)); compatible encoders put related inputs near each other. Similarity reflects the encoder's training objective and may miss negation, numeric differences, or domain terms.

articles.explanation: Prompt injection occurs when untrusted text attempts to redirect model behavior across a trust boundary. articles.title: Agent loop
articles.definition: An agent loop repeatedly decides, requests actions, observes results, updates state and decides whether to stop.
articles.explanation: An agent loop repeatedly decides, requests actions, observes results, updates state and decides whether to stop. The runtime sends state and allowed tools to the model, validates and executes requests, appends observations, and applies termination checks. Each iteration consumes latency and tokens; tool success and goal completion require explicit verification.

articles.quickAnswer: An agent loop repeatedly decides, requests actions, observes results, updates state and decides whether to stop. The runtime sends state and allowed tools to the model, validates and executes requests, appends observations, and applies termination checks.
articles.deepDive:
An agent loop gives a model repeated opportunities to choose an action based on what just happened, rather than committing to a fixed plan once. Start with an objective, canonical task state and a restricted tool catalog. At each iteration the runtime assembles a bounded context, asks the model for a next action or final response, validates the requested arguments and authorizes the operation. The runtime executes the tool, records a typed observation and updates state before the next decision. The model requests actions; it does not directly invoke the application's functions.

State should distinguish user requirements, verified facts, hypotheses, pending operations and completed results. A transcript can be useful context, but authorization, resource budgets and durable progress should live in typed application fields. Long runs need checkpoints and stable operation IDs so recovery can reconcile uncertain effects rather than repeat them blindly.

Termination has multiple layers: the model can propose that the task is done, the application verifies the actual success condition, and hard runtime limits stop excessive steps, elapsed time, tokens or tool expense. Detect repeated state-action pairs without progress and distinguish recoverable transient failures from invalid requests or absent information. Use bounded retries with jitter where appropriate; request clarification or escalate when evidence is insufficient.

For a support agent, searching policy, looking up an account and drafting a response can fit the loop. Refund eligibility and authorization should remain deterministic boundaries. A timeout after issuing a refund is an uncertain outcome, not proof that no refund happened. Compare task success, duplicate effects, policy adherence, latency and cost against a simpler workflow. The best production design often grants autonomy only at the points where changing observations justify it.

questions.prompt: A retrieved document tells the assistant to export customer records. What controls belong outside the model? Choose the best engineering response.
questions.referenceAnswer: Prompt injection occurs when untrusted text attempts to redirect model behavior across a trust boundary. An attacker places commands in retrieved content or tool output; the model may treat those commands as instructions. For example: A retrieved document tells the assistant to export customer records. What controls belong outside the model? Enforce least-privilege tools, application authorization, data isolation, egress limits, and approvals bound to exact operations.

questions.prompt: An agent repeats an obsolete address from earlier conversation. What changes help? Choose the best engineering response.

questions.prompt: A ten-step agent fails far more often than its single-step benchmark predicts. What should you measure? Choose the best engineering response.
questions.referenceAnswer: Multi-step execution can amplify small local mistakes through dependent actions. If n independent required steps each succeed with probability p, total success is p to the n; real errors are often correlated. For example: A ten-step agent fails far more often than its single-step benchmark predicts. What should you measure? Inspect whole trajectories, dependencies and correlated failures; add verification at critical boundaries and simplify unnecessary steps.

questions.prompt: A cited policy is outdated but every sentence is supported by it. Which quality dimension failed? Choose the best engineering response.
questions.referenceAnswer: Grounding ties claims to available evidence; abstention declines to answer when support is insufficient. Retrieve relevant facts, generate constrained claims, verify support, and communicate uncertainty or request clarification. Decompose an answer into verifiable claims; check entailment from evidence; report supported claims divided by evaluable claims. For example: Retrieval recall is high but the answer adds a nonexistent exception. What failed? Inspect generation prompts, conflicting evidence and claim-level support; compare oracle context before changing retrieval.

questions.prompt: A predictable three-step task has been replaced by an agent and becomes unreliable. What would you change? Choose the best engineering response.
questions.referenceAnswer: A workflow follows predefined orchestration while an agent lets a model choose some actions based on goals and observations. Production systems often embed a bounded model-driven decision loop within deterministic routing and validation. For example: A predictable three-step task has been replaced by an agent and becomes unreliable. What would you change? Restore deterministic steps where requirements are fixed and reserve model decisions for genuine ambiguity; evaluate whole-task success.

questions.prompt: An agent repeats the same unsuccessful search indefinitely. How would you stop and recover it? Choose the best engineering response.
questions.referenceAnswer: An agent loop repeatedly decides, requests actions, observes results, updates state and decides whether to stop. The runtime sends state and allowed tools to the model, validates and executes requests, appends observations, and applies termination checks. For example: An agent repeats the same unsuccessful search indefinitely. How would you stop and recover it? Cap steps, wall time and tokens; detect repeated state-action pairs; classify the failure and ask for clarification or take an alternative.
questions.quickAnswer: An agent loop repeatedly decides, requests actions, observes results, updates state and decides whether to stop. The runtime sends state and allowed tools to the model, validates and executes requests, appends observations, and applies termination checks.

answers.core: An agent loop repeatedly decides, requests actions, observes results, updates state and decides whether to stop.
answers.strong: An agent loop repeatedly decides, requests actions, observes results, updates state and decides whether to stop. The runtime sends state and allowed tools to the model, validates and executes requests, appends observations, and applies termination checks. For example: An agent repeats the same unsuccessful search indefinitely. How would you stop and recover it? Cap steps, wall time and tokens; detect repeated state-action pairs; classify the failure and ask for clarification or take an alternative.
answers.expert:
An agent loop gives a model repeated opportunities to choose an action based on what just happened, rather than committing to a fixed plan once. Start with an objective, canonical task state and a restricted tool catalog. At each iteration the runtime assembles a bounded context, asks the model for a next action or final response, validates the requested arguments and authorizes the operation. The runtime executes the tool, records a typed observation and updates state before the next decision. The model requests actions; it does not directly invoke the application's functions.

State should distinguish user requirements, verified facts, hypotheses, pending operations and completed results. A transcript can be useful context, but authorization, resource budgets and durable progress should live in typed application fields. Long runs need checkpoints and stable operation IDs so recovery can reconcile uncertain effects rather than repeat them blindly.

Termination has multiple layers: the model can propose that the task is done, the application verifies the actual success condition, and hard runtime limits stop excessive steps, elapsed time, tokens or tool expense. Detect repeated state-action pairs without progress and distinguish recoverable transient failures from invalid requests or absent information. Use bounded retries with jitter where appropriate; request clarification or escalate when evidence is insufficient.

For a support agent, searching policy, looking up an account and drafting a response can fit the loop. Refund eligibility and authorization should remain deterministic boundaries. A timeout after issuing a refund is an uncertain outcome, not proof that no refund happened. Compare task success, duplicate effects, policy adherence, latency and cost against a simpler workflow. The best production design often grants autonomy only at the points where changing observations justify it.

questions.prompt: A planner assumes a tool succeeded even though it returned an error. What would you enforce? Choose the best engineering response.
questions.referenceAnswer: ReAct interleaves reasoning-oriented decisions with actions and observations to adapt to external information. The runtime alternates model decisions and tool results; useful traces capture actions, inputs, outcomes and state transitions. For example: A planner assumes a tool succeeded even though it returned an error. What would you enforce? Use typed observations with status fields, require outcome checks before dependent actions, and trace decisions without relying on private chain-of-thought.

questions.prompt: The process crashes after a payment succeeds but before state is saved. What should recovery do? Choose the best engineering response.
questions.referenceAnswer: A checkpoint stores sufficient execution state to continue a run from a known boundary after interruption. Persist task identity, current state, completed steps and pending work transactionally; reload the latest committed checkpoint on recovery. For example: The process crashes after a payment succeeds but before state is saved. What should recovery do? Reconcile with the external service using an idempotency key or operation ID before retrying; never infer payment failure from a missing checkpoint.

questions.prompt: A team claims connecting MCP automatically makes every tool safe. What responsibilities remain? Choose the best engineering response.

questions.prompt: A traffic spike creates hours of queued requests. What controls protect usefulness? Choose the best engineering response.

questions.prompt: Design a enterprise rag platform. Requirements: Support multiple teams, tenant isolation, fresh content, audit trails and predictable latency. Explain components, data flow, failure recovery, scaling, trade-offs and evaluation.
questions.referenceAnswer: Support multiple teams, tenant isolation, fresh content, audit trails and predictable latency. Permission-aware connectors → validated ingestion queue → tenant-tagged index → authorized retrieval → rerank → cited generation → audit trace. Pre-filtering protects context; fine-grained ACL changes complicate index and cache invalidation. Failure cases: Cross-tenant cache reuse or stale ACLs leak data; connector failures silently drop documents. questions.referenceAnswer: Run for hours, recover after restart, pause for approval and honor cancellation. Durable job queue → leased worker → checkpointed graph → idempotent tool ledger → pending approvals → recovery reconciler. At-least-once work with idempotency is practical; cross-service exactly-once behavior needs stronger coordination. Failure cases: Crash after remote success before checkpoint; expired worker commits after another worker resumes. Evaluation: Inject crashes before and after effects; score recovery, duplicate effects, cancellation latency and budget compliance.

questions.referenceAnswer: Provide visibility into long-running tasks, stalled steps, pending approvals and resource use. Run registry → event stream → span store → state projection → alert rules → user timeline with cancellation controls. Detailed traces aid diagnosis but need redaction and bounded retention; sampling can miss rare failures. Failure cases: A heartbeat stays alive while no task progress occurs; duplicate events corrupt totals. Evaluation: Test stalled-state detection, event deduplication, privacy controls and reconciliation against persisted checkpoints.

questions.prompt: Design a secure mcp gateway. Requirements: Expose approved internal capabilities through MCP while preserving tenant and downstream authorization. Explain components, data flow, failure recovery, scaling, trade-offs and evaluation.
questions.referenceAnswer: Expose approved internal capabilities through MCP while preserving tenant and downstream authorization. Host/client → authenticated transport → scoped catalog → policy gateway → downstream adapters → auditable results. Central policy improves consistency but adds latency and a shared failure point; direct integration remains useful for narrow needs. Failure cases: Confused-deputy token forwarding, untrusted server instructions or overbroad tool discovery. Evaluation: Test token audience, tenant isolation, exact-operation consent, timeouts and protocol-compatible failure responses.

questions.prompt: Design a model routing service. Requirements: Choose local or hosted model strategies by quality requirements, capacity and budget with explicit policy. Explain components, data flow, failure recovery, scaling, trade-offs and evaluation.
questions.referenceAnswer: Choose local or hosted model strategies by quality requirements, capacity and budget with explicit policy. Request contract → deterministic routing → candidate model → validation → bounded fallback → metrics and versioned cache. Cheap routing may increase retries; fallbacks must preserve schema and privacy constraints. Failure cases: Fallback violates output contract, sends sensitive data to a prohibited provider or loops during an outage. Evaluation: Evaluate each route on quality, allowed data handling, total cost per success and tail latency.

questions.prompt: Design a evaluation-aware release system. Requirements: Deploy prompt and model changes safely with rollback and monitored task outcomes. Explain components, data flow, failure recovery, scaling, trade-offs and evaluation.
questions.referenceAnswer: Deploy prompt and model changes safely with rollback and monitored task outcomes. Versioned artifacts → protected holdout evaluations → safety gates → staged rollout → slice monitoring → automatic or operator rollback. Offline gates offer repeatability; live monitoring detects distribution shifts but requires privacy-aware sampling. Failure cases: Overall engagement rises while a critical task slice fails; rollback references a missing model artifact. Evaluation: Track task success, safety incidents, latency, cost and rollback effectiveness against declared release criteria.
